essays.question: Discuss the role of the internet in promoting free speech.

versions.text:
Not long ago, a handful of newspapers and television channels decided which opinions reached the public, but today anyone with a phone can publish a message to the world. This essay will explain two key ways in which the internet promotes free speech: by giving ordinary people a platform and by making it easier to share information and organise.

First and foremost, the internet gives ordinary people a platform that no one controls. Anyone with a connection can publish opinions, share news and organise with others without needing a newspaper or broadcaster, which helps those whose views are ignored or suppressed. A blogger who posts photographs of illegal logging, for example, can reach thousands of people even if the local newspaper stays silent. In countries where the press is restricted, citizens use social media and messaging apps to report events and debate openly, and minority groups can find audiences that traditional media would not give them. Voices from remote regions can be heard worldwide.

In addition, the internet makes it easier to share information and to organise. Posts and videos can spread to millions in hours, protests and petitions can be arranged quickly, and people with similar concerns can find one another across borders. Encrypted tools also protect journalists and activists. However, the same freedom brings problems. Rumour, harassment and hate speech spread easily, and some governments block websites or monitor users to silence critics. Free speech online therefore needs protection from both abuse and censorship, with clear laws, transparency from platforms and digital skills for users who must decide which sources to trust.

To sum up, the internet promotes free speech by giving everyone a voice and by making information easy to share, although it requires careful safeguards. For these reasons, open access to it should be protected.

essays.question: Many people say that migration benefits the host country. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Millions of people move to other countries every year to work, study or escape danger, and many people say that migration benefits the host country. I agree with this view, since migrants fill gaps in the workforce and contribute to the economy and culture, although the benefits depend on good planning.

To begin with, migrants fill gaps in the workforce and contribute to the economy. They work in hospitals, farms, construction and technology where employers cannot find enough staff, pay taxes, start businesses and help ageing countries to keep their workforce. A hospital that depends on nurses from abroad, for example, would struggle to keep its wards open without them. Studies in several countries have shown that immigrants often take jobs that local people are unwilling or unable to do, and they spend money, which creates demand for goods and services. Skilled migrants also bring knowledge and links with other countries that help trade and innovation.

Furthermore, migration enriches society. New foods, languages and ideas increase diversity and creativity, and contact between cultures can reduce prejudice. However, migration brings challenges that need planning. Housing, schools and health services may come under pressure in areas where many newcomers settle, wages for some low-paid local workers may be affected, and integration is difficult if newcomers do not speak the language or face discrimination. These problems are manageable if governments invest in services, offer language classes, recognise foreign qualifications and enforce laws against discrimination. Well-managed migration benefits both newcomers and residents, while neglect can cause resentment.

In conclusion, I agree that migration benefits the host country, because it fills workforce gaps and enriches society, provided that it is managed with proper support for integration.

essays.question: Discuss how media coverage affects public opinion during elections.

versions.text:
Most voters never meet a candidate and learn about them through newspapers, television and the internet, so media coverage has great power in elections. This essay will explain two key ways in which media coverage affects public opinion during elections: by deciding which issues voters think about, and by shaping how they see candidates.

First and foremost, media coverage decides which issues voters think about and how they see candidates. By choosing what to report, how to frame it and whom to interview, newspapers and broadcasters shape priorities. If the media spend weeks on immigration and little on health care, voters may come to feel that immigration is the main issue, whatever their own concerns. A headline that announces which candidate is ahead, for example, can encourage some voters to follow the winner and others to stay at home. Coverage also affects how voters judge a candidate's personality, since a single mistake that is replayed endlessly can damage a reputation more than years of careful policy work.

In addition, the way in which elections are reported often favours drama over detail. Coverage that treats the campaign as a horse race, focusing on opinion polls and personal conflicts, can crowd out discussion of policy, and partisan outlets may present only one side. However, a diverse media offers corrections. Independent fact-checking, public broadcasters with a duty of balance, and a free press that investigates candidates from all parties help voters to form their own views. Citizens should also compare several sources and be aware that every outlet has its own perspective.

To sum up, media coverage strongly affects public opinion during elections by shaping priorities and images, so diversity and honesty in the media are essential to democracy.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that social media increases political awareness?

versions.text:
Politicians now post on social media every day, and some people believe that these platforms make citizens more politically aware. I largely agree, since they make information faster and easier to share, although awareness does not always mean understanding.

To begin with, social media makes political information faster, cheaper and easier to share. News, debates and campaign messages reach young people who rarely read newspapers, and ordinary citizens can question politicians directly. A student who sees a politician's speech shared by friends, for example, may follow the story further, although she may also see only views that she already agrees with. Hashtags and live videos bring attention to issues that traditional media might ignore, and campaigns on topics such as climate change or equality have reached millions. Participation has risen in several countries as young voters learn about elections and registration deadlines online.

Furthermore, social media allows people to discuss politics and to organise. Online communities help citizens to find others who share their concerns and to join petitions and demonstrations. However, awareness is not always understanding. Algorithms tend to show people content that confirms their existing views, creating echo chambers, and false stories can spread faster than corrections. Engagement may also be shallow, such as pressing a like button rather than taking action. To get the full benefit, users should compare several sources, schools should teach media literacy, and platforms should be more transparent about how they rank content.

In conclusion, social media increases political awareness to a large extent by making information accessible, but its benefits depend on users and platforms ensuring that it is accurate and balanced.

essays.question: Discuss how technology influences voting behaviour.

versions.text:
In recent elections, campaigns have been fought as much on phones and laptops as on doorsteps, and technology has changed how people decide whom to vote for. This essay will explain two key ways in which technology influences voting behaviour: by changing how voters get information and by changing how campaigns reach them.

First and foremost, technology shapes how voters learn about candidates. Social media spreads both information and false stories, and online tools make registration and research easier. A student who looks up the policies of every party in a few minutes, for example, is better informed than a voter of fifty years ago who relied on a single newspaper. Websites compare manifestos, fact-checkers examine claims, and live streaming lets voters watch debates wherever they are. However, the same tools can mislead, since search results and feeds may show people only what confirms their opinions, and deliberately false stories can influence undecided voters.

In addition, technology changes how campaigns reach voters. Parties use data to target messages at individuals, based on age, job and interests, so that a voter who receives advertisements aimed at his age, job and neighbourhood, for example, sees a very different campaign from his neighbour. Targeted messages can motivate groups who are normally ignored, but they can also be misleading, since the public cannot easily see or challenge what others are being told. Automated accounts can create the impression of widespread support. Voters therefore need skills to judge sources, and regulators should require campaigns to be transparent about who is paying for advertisements and how data are used.

To sum up, technology influences voting behaviour by changing how people learn about politics and how campaigns persuade them. For these reasons, it deserves both encouragement and careful regulation.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that voting should be compulsory?

versions.text:
In some countries, citizens who do not vote are fined, and some people argue that voting should be compulsory. I disagree with this view, since compelling people to vote treats a right as a duty and may produce uninformed choices, although I would like turnout to be high.

To begin with, compelling people to vote treats a right as a duty and may produce uninformed choices. Citizens who are forced to attend a polling station may vote randomly or leave the paper blank, resent the state and lose the sense that voting is a free expression of opinion. A person who dislikes every candidate but must still go to the polling station, for example, may simply tick a name at random. Such votes do not make the result more representative, and they may favour candidates whose names are more familiar. In a free society, the right to take part in politics should include the right to choose not to take part, as with other freedoms such as speech and religion.

Furthermore, compulsion treats the symptom, not the cause. Low turnout usually reflects distrust, dissatisfaction with the choice offered or practical difficulties, and forcing people to vote does not address these problems. Supporters point out that compulsory voting increases turnout and makes governments more representative, as in Australia, where participation is very high. That is a real advantage. However, the same result can be achieved by making voting easier and more meaningful through weekend elections, early and postal voting, better civic education and more responsive politics. Fines also fall hardest on those with the least money.

In conclusion, I disagree that voting should be compulsory, because it limits freedom and produces uninformed votes, and the focus should be on making participation easier and more attractive.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on emergency services or on prevention programs? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be spent mainly on emergency services or on prevention programmes. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of emergency services argue that they save lives at the moment when everything else has failed. Fire crews, ambulances and rescue teams reach people in danger within minutes, and some accidents and disasters happen however much prevention is in place. A person who suffers a heart attack, for example, may survive only if an ambulance arrives within minutes. Cutting these services would put lives at immediate risk, and the public expects the state to respond whenever help is needed. Emergency workers also provide reassurance, because people feel safer when they know that help will come quickly. Well-equipped services also deal with events that no prevention could stop, such as earthquakes and sudden illness.

On the other hand, supporters of prevention point out that it stops harm before it happens and costs far less than repairing damage. Safety education, building standards, health screening and crime-prevention programmes reduce the number of emergencies in the first place, and the savings continue year after year. A town that builds flood walls and drains, for example, may avoid damage that would cost far more to repair after every storm. Prevention also reduces suffering that cannot be measured in money, such as injuries, bereavement and lost homes. Preventing a fire is better than extinguishing it.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that a balanced budget is best: emergency services must be fully funded because they are essential, but a growing share should go to prevention because it reduces the need for emergency help.

essays.question: How can governments make voting more accessible? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
In many democracies, a large share of eligible citizens never vote, and some of them are kept away by practical obstacles such as long queues, strict deadlines and inconvenient hours. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on making it easier to cast a vote and on making information and registration simpler.

To begin with, governments should remove the practical obstacles that stop people from voting. More polling stations, early and postal voting, weekend or holiday elections, transport for older and disabled voters and automatic registration make it easier to take part. A nurse who works night shifts, for example, can vote during a week of early voting instead of missing the single election day. Longer opening hours and mobile polling stations in rural areas help people who live far from a town. Voting by post or secure online systems can suit people who are away from home, such as students and workers abroad, provided that safeguards against fraud are in place.

In addition, authorities should make registration and information simple. Automatic or same-day registration removes a barrier that stops many young people and those who move home often, and reminders by text message can encourage participation. Clear guides in several languages and plain language help new citizens and people with limited education to understand how to vote. Equally important, polling places should be accessible to wheelchair users, with assistance available for those who are blind or have difficulty reading. Measures like these cost little compared with the democratic benefits, and they help ensure that governments represent the whole population.

In conclusion, widening opportunities to vote and simplifying registration and information offer the most realistic way of making voting more accessible.

essays.question: What are the causes of low voter turnout? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
In many democracies, fewer than two-thirds of eligible voters take part in elections, and in some local elections the figure is far lower. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Low turnout reflects distrust, a feeling that votes do not matter and practical obstacles. Voters who believe that politicians are all the same or that the result will not change their lives see little point in taking part, and registration rules, long queues and working hours make voting inconvenient. A worker who sees a queue of two hours outside the polling station, for example, may decide that his time is better spent elsewhere. In addition, young people and those on low incomes, who often feel ignored by parties, are the least likely to vote, and weak civic education leaves many unsure how the system works or why it matters. As a result, their interests are underrepresented, which increases their sense of exclusion in a damaging cycle.

To address this issue, governments should make voting easier and politics more relevant. Early and postal voting, weekend elections and automatic registration remove practical barriers, while civic education in schools teaches young people how decisions are made and why participation matters. In addition, parties should engage directly with young and poorer communities, and electoral reform, such as more proportional systems, can make votes count more. Greater transparency about money in politics and tougher action against corruption would help to rebuild trust. Campaigns by independent bodies can also remind people of election dates and explain how to vote.

In conclusion, low voter turnout stems mainly from distrust and inconvenience, but easier voting, civic education and more responsive politics offer a realistic way forward.

essays.question: What are the causes of corruption in public office? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
Corruption by officials, from small bribes to large-scale theft of public money, damages development in many countries. This essay will analyse the principal causes of corruption in public office and propose realistic solutions.

Corruption grows where power is unchecked and punishment is weak. Officials with low pay and wide discretion are tempted by bribes, secrecy hides wrongdoing, and a culture that tolerates favours makes it seem normal. An official who is paid very little and controls permits, for example, may be tempted to ask for a bribe to approve an application. In addition, weak courts and poorly supported anti-corruption agencies mean that offenders rarely face punishment, and complicated rules create more opportunities for officials to demand payment for ordinary services. When citizens expect to pay bribes, corruption becomes self-reinforcing, and public money is wasted while trust in government falls.

To address this issue, governments should combine transparency, independent oversight and certain punishment. Open contracts and published budgets expose abuse, independent agencies investigate without fear, fair salaries reduce temptation, and protected whistleblowers make reporting safe. Simplifying procedures and moving services online reduces the face-to-face contact in which bribes are asked for. In addition, courts must be independent, so that powerful people cannot escape punishment, and a free press and education can build a culture that rejects corruption. Reform takes time, but countries that have reduced corruption, by following such steps, have seen public services improve and investment rise.

In conclusion, corruption in public office stems mainly from unchecked power, low pay and weak punishment, but transparency, independent oversight and fair rules offer a realistic way forward.

essays.question: To what extent should governments control online hate speech? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Online platforms allow people to insult others about their race, religion or origin in front of millions, and some argue that governments should control online hate speech. I largely agree, since it causes real harm and companies cannot be left to regulate themselves, although controls must be carefully limited.

To begin with, online hate speech causes real harm and should be limited by law. Abuse aimed at a person's race, religion or identity can drive victims offline, spread fear and sometimes lead to violence. A woman who receives hundreds of abusive messages about her religion, for example, may stop speaking in public altogether, which damages free expression rather than protecting it. Hatred spread online has been linked to attacks on minorities in several countries, and young people who see such content may come to accept it as normal. Companies that profit from engagement have little reason to remove content that attracts attention, so they cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Furthermore, governments are the only bodies able to set clear, consistent rules and to enforce them across platforms. Laws can require companies to remove illegal content quickly, report seriously dangerous threats and publish information on how they moderate. However, controls have risks. Definitions of hate speech can be vague, and governments may use them to silence criticism or minority opinions. Rules must therefore be narrow and clearly defined, restricted to threats, incitement to violence and abuse that targets people for who they are, with oversight by independent courts and a right of appeal. Education about respectful behaviour online is also important, because laws alone cannot change attitudes.

In conclusion, governments should control online hate speech to a large extent, because it harms people and platforms will not solve the problem themselves, provided that the rules are narrow and protect legitimate debate.

essays.question: Some people believe that public protests are a vital part of democracy. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Marches, strikes and sit-ins are familiar parts of political life, and opinions differ on whether public protests are a vital part of democracy. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that peaceful protest lets citizens speak between elections. Marches and demonstrations show politicians how strongly people feel, have helped to win rights such as votes for women and civil rights, and give a voice to groups that are ignored by parties and newspapers. A peaceful march of thousands of people through the capital, for example, shows politicians that an issue cannot be ignored. In a democracy, power belongs to the people, and the freedom to gather and express views openly is itself a basic right. Where protest is banned, governments often grow less accountable, which is why authoritarian regimes fear it so much.

On the other hand, critics point out that protests can cause disruption and sometimes violence. Roads and businesses may be blocked, ordinary people may be harmed, and the small group who take part may not represent the majority. Disruption or violence can also turn public opinion against a cause. In a democracy, there are other channels, such as elections, petitions, courts and elected representatives, through which concerns can be raised and settled by law. Decisions made under the pressure of crowds may not be well considered, and protests can be organised by groups that are well-funded rather than widely supported.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that peaceful protest is a vital part of democracy, because it gives citizens a voice, provided that it remains lawful and respects the rights of others.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on emergency response or on long-term prevention? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Floods, earthquakes and storms cause enormous damage every year, and opinions differ on whether governments should focus on emergency response after a disaster or on long-term prevention. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of emergency response argue that rescue and relief save lives at the moment of greatest need. Search teams, field hospitals, food and shelter must be ready within hours, and when a disaster strikes the public expects an immediate and visible response. A family trapped by floodwater, for example, can only be rescued by trained crews with boats and helicopters, however many defences were planned. Emergency response also protects order, since people who are hungry and without shelter may panic. Some disasters, such as earthquakes, cannot be predicted, so response capacity is always necessary.

On the other hand, supporters of long-term prevention point out that preparing in advance reduces damage and costs far less than repairing it. Flood defences, strict building standards, early warning systems and better land planning mean that fewer people are in danger when a hazard arrives. A town that builds flood walls and drains, for example, may avoid damage that would cost far more to repair after every storm. Climate change is also making disasters more frequent, so investment in resilience becomes increasingly urgent. Money spent on prevention often protects homes, jobs and public services as well as lives, and the benefits continue for decades.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that prevention should receive the larger share of long-term spending, because it reduces losses, while a well-funded emergency response must be maintained for the events that cannot be prevented.

Chuẩn bị trước giảm thiệt hại và rẻ hơn sửa chữa: đê chống lũ, tiêu chuẩn xây dựng nghiêm, cảnh báo sớm, quy hoạch đất; biến đổi khí hậu làm thiên tai thường hơn nên đầu tư khả năng chống chịu cấp bách; bảo vệ cả nhà cửa, việc làm, dịch vụ công; lợi ích kéo dài hàng chục năm.
Phòng ngừa nên nhận phần lớn hơn của chi tiêu dài hạn nhưng vẫn duy trì ứng phó đủ kinh phí cho sự kiện không phòng được.

essays.question: Discuss how language policy can affect national unity.

versions.text:
Many countries are home to several languages, and governments must decide which to use in schools, courts and official documents. This essay will explain two key ways in which language policy can affect national unity: by helping people to communicate and share opportunities, and by affecting how minority groups feel about their place in the nation.

First and foremost, a shared language can unite a country, but forcing it can divide. A common language gives everyone access to education, jobs and public services, and it makes it easier for people from different regions to understand one another and to take part in national debates. In a country where citizens speak several languages and cannot communicate, the lack of a common tongue may create separate communities that know little about each other. A national language taught in all schools, for example, lets a young person from a remote village apply for a job in the capital. Shared language can also be a symbol of belonging.

In addition, language policy affects how minority groups feel. Suppressing minority languages makes people feel that their identity is threatened, and may produce resentment and even separatist movements. A region whose road signs and schools use both the national and the local language, for example, lets residents feel that their culture is respected. Evidence from countries with several official languages suggests that bilingual policies can maintain unity while keeping diversity. However, they require resources for teachers, translators and materials. Governments should therefore promote a common language while protecting others, so that all citizens feel valued.

To sum up, language policy can strengthen or weaken national unity depending on whether it respects diversity as well as promoting shared communication. For these reasons, policies should be designed with care.

essays.question: Some believe that compulsory military service benefits society. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Some countries require young adults to spend a year or more in the armed forces, and some believe that compulsory military service benefits society. I agree only to a limited extent, since it can teach discipline and bring citizens together, although it has serious costs and professional forces are often more effective.

To begin with, compulsory service can teach discipline and bring citizens from different backgrounds together. Recruits learn teamwork, fitness and practical skills and meet people they would never otherwise meet. A recruit from a farming village sharing a barracks with a student from the capital, for example, learns about a very different way of life, which may reduce prejudice and strengthen national feeling. Service can also give young people who are drifting a sense of direction and training in trades such as mechanics or first aid. In countries facing real military threats, a large trained reserve provides security.

However, the costs are significant. Recruits lose time for study and work, and many do not want to be there, which can reduce morale and make forces less effective than smaller professional armies that are well trained and motivated. Compulsion limits personal freedom, and some people object on grounds of conscience. Unequal treatment of men and women, or of rich and poor who find ways to avoid service, can create resentment. If the aim is to build skills and community, other forms of national service, such as volunteering in hospitals or environmental projects, may bring similar benefits without the need to carry weapons. Governments should therefore weigh benefits against costs carefully.

In conclusion, compulsory military service benefits society only to a limited extent, because the advantages of discipline and social mixing are outweighed in many countries by the costs and by better alternatives.

essays.question: Many people think that youth activism is important for social change. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
From climate strikes to campaigns for equality, young people are leading many protest movements, and many people think that youth activism is important for social change. I agree with this view, since young people bring energy, fresh ideas and a long-term stake, although their impact depends on how well they work with others.

To begin with, young people bring energy, fresh ideas and a long-term stake to social change. They will live with the consequences of today's decisions on climate, housing and jobs, they are skilled at using social media, and they often challenge habits that older generations accept. Students who leave lessons to demand action on climate change, for example, can put the issue on the front page of newspapers and force politicians to respond. Young people are also less tied to existing institutions and interests, so they are more willing to suggest bold solutions. Many past reforms, from student movements against war to campaigns for civil rights, began with the energy of the young.

Furthermore, activism teaches young people civic skills that last a lifetime, such as organising, debating and cooperating, and many activists later become community leaders or politicians. However, activism has limits. Young people may lack experience of how laws are made, and online campaigns can be shallow, with likes and shares that do not lead to action. Movements can fade when attention moves on. Their impact is greatest when they work with experienced organisations, build clear demands and keep their efforts going over time, and when adults listen to them seriously. Schools and governments can help by creating youth councils and consultations.

In conclusion, I agree that youth activism is important for social change, because young people bring energy and ideas, provided that their efforts are sustained and taken seriously.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on disaster preparedness? Use examples.

versions.text:
Earthquakes, floods, storms and epidemics can strike any country, and some governments invest heavily in being ready for them. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on disaster preparedness: protection of lives and health, and reduced economic damage and faster recovery.

First and foremost, preparing for disasters saves lives and reduces injuries. Early warning systems, evacuation plans, strict building codes and stored supplies mean that fewer people are hurt and communities recover faster. A country in an earthquake zone that enforces strict building codes, for example, loses far fewer lives than one that does not, because houses and schools remain standing. Regular drills teach residents what to do, and clear communication prevents panic. As a result, hospitals are not overwhelmed, and people receive help sooner. Communities that know their risks and have rescue teams trained in advance are better able to protect their most vulnerable members.

In addition, preparedness reduces economic damage and speeds recovery. Every unit of money spent on preparation can save many times as much on repair, because protected homes, factories and roads suffer less harm and businesses can reopen sooner. Insurance schemes and emergency funds ensure that families are not pushed into poverty. Public confidence also rises when people see that their government is ready, which supports stability and investment. Although preparing requires investment in equipment, training and planning, and some of it may never be used, the cost is small compared with the losses from a major disaster. Coastal countries that built sea walls and warning systems after severe storms, for instance, have been able to protect cities that were once highly vulnerable.

To sum up, disaster preparedness brings clear benefits to a country, above all lives saved and lower economic losses. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Some believe that national service improves civic responsibility. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
In several countries, young people are required or encouraged to give a year of their time to national service, either in the armed forces or in community roles, and some believe that national service improves civic responsibility. I largely agree, since it can teach young people to serve others, although it works only if the service is meaningful.

To begin with, national service can strengthen civic responsibility if it is meaningful. Young people who spend a year helping in hospitals, schools or emergency teams see the needs of their community, learn to cooperate and often keep volunteering afterwards. A school leaver who spends a year helping in a care home, for example, may continue to volunteer for years afterwards, and will understand ageing and illness far better than a person who has never been in such a place. Working with people from different backgrounds also reduces prejudice and builds a sense that citizens depend on one another. Experience of duty teaches that rights come with responsibilities.

Furthermore, service gives young people practical skills and confidence that make them more active citizens, such as teamwork, leadership and problem-solving. Those who take part often feel more connected to their country and more willing to vote, volunteer and take part in public life. However, the effect depends on design. Pointless or forced tasks may create resentment instead, and compulsion may make some young people dislike the idea of service. Programmes should offer real choices between military, social and environmental roles, provide training and recognition, and ensure that those with disabilities or caring duties can take part in suitable ways. Evidence of long-term effects on civic behaviour is still limited, so schemes should be evaluated.

In conclusion, national service improves civic responsibility to a large extent when it is meaningful and offers choice, but poorly designed schemes can have the opposite effect.

essays.question: Discuss the role of technology in improving free speech.

versions.text:
Mobile phones, social media and translation tools have changed how people speak out, and technology is often described as a friend of free speech. This essay will outline two key ways in which technology improves free speech: by widening access and by protecting those who speak.

First and foremost, technology widens access to speech and to audiences. Cheap smartphones, video platforms and blogs give ordinary people a platform that no one controls, so a farmer, a student or a nurse can describe what is happening in their community. Translation tools allow messages to cross language barriers, and live streaming lets witnesses show events as they happen. A student who films an incident and posts it online, for example, may expose abuse that official media would never mention. Because a single post can reach thousands, groups that were once ignored can now organise petitions and campaigns.

In addition, technology can protect people who speak. Encrypted messaging allows journalists, activists and ordinary citizens to communicate safely under hostile regimes, and tools that hide identity help whistleblowers to share evidence without being traced. Archives and cloud storage keep records safe even if an authority tries to delete them. However, technology also creates new threats. Governments use filtering, facial recognition and spyware to monitor critics, and platforms can silence voices through automated moderation or opaque rules. Online abuse can force people into silence. Technology therefore improves free speech only when it is accompanied by privacy laws, open rules for platforms and independent courts.

To sum up, technology improves free speech by widening access and offering protection, provided that it is governed by fair laws. For these reasons, the right to use secure technology should be defended.

essays.question: Some people say that censorship is a waste of time and money. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Some governments block websites, ban books and control newspapers, and some people say that censorship is a waste of time and money. I largely agree, since broad censorship rarely achieves its aim, although a narrow set of controls can be justified.

To begin with, broad censorship wastes money and rarely achieves its aim. Determined people find ways around blocks, officials must spend large sums on monitoring, and hiding information damages public trust. A blocked website, for example, is often accessible again within hours through a different address or a virtual private network. Banning a book or film often increases curiosity, so that it is read or watched more widely than it would otherwise have been. Large teams of staff and technology are needed to scan content, and mistakes are common, so legitimate information is blocked together with harmful material. The cost could be used for schools or hospitals.

Furthermore, censorship has serious side effects. It stops citizens from learning facts about their own government, hides problems that need to be solved and teaches people to distrust official information. Societies that allow open debate tend to find mistakes earlier and correct them. However, a narrow set of content, such as child abuse, direct incitement to violence and terrorist recruitment, justifies control, because the harm is severe and immediate. Even in these cases, rules should be clear, decisions should be made by courts or independent bodies, and the public should be able to challenge them. Education and media literacy are often more effective than bans in protecting people from harmful or false information.

In conclusion, general censorship is largely a waste of time and money, but carefully targeted restrictions on the most harmful material can be justified.
